articles.title: US government bans new foreign-made humanoids, robot dogs, and solar inverters, citing risks to national security | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The ban largely affects U.S. imports from China, which currently dominates the global market for making humanoid robots and solar inverters.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is banning the import of new foreign-made humanoid robots, robot dogs, and power inverters, citing an “unacceptable” threat to national security. The move largely affects imports from China, which currently has the vast majority of the global market share.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced the ban on Tuesday, saying that devices made overseas could be remotely controlled or used for surveillance by foreign governments, or otherwise used in cyberattacks.

The FCC said that exceptions would be granted if the government finds that a device does not pose a risk to U.S. national security.

The U.S. government has long accused China of hacking into U.S. businesses to steal data and preparing to launch future cyberattacks for its own military gains, such as an anticipated invasion of Taiwan. But the U.S. has also long warned that the risk of Chinese ownership alone could allow Beijing to force a company to spy on Americans or remotely tamper with their products. The U.S. government has similar legal powers .

Humanoid robots, the class of robots that move similarly to humans, are far from mainstream and are still in early development . There were around 15,000 humanoid robots shipped worldwide in 2025, with each of China’s two largest robot makers accounting for the majority of those shipments.

Power inverters are far more commonly used in U.S. households to connect solar and other renewable energy systems to the wider power grid. Existing devices in homes and installations are unaffected by the ban, the FCC said.

The ban is the latest in a series of actions taken by the U.S. government against China in recent years, including a U.S. government ban on TikTok that forced it into the hands of U.S. investors, plus bans on a broad swath of foreign-made consumer routers , and Chinese surveillance equipment makers Hikvision and Dahua, which have been linked to human rights abuses .

Beijing rebuffed the FCC’s ban, with a Foreign Ministry spokesperson quoted by the Associated Press as saying that China will use “all measures necessary” to protect its businesses.

Chinese president Xi Jinping is expected to meet President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C., during a planned state visit in September.

articles.title: Jobs that earn six figures without going to college (and why they are rare)
articles.summary: As college costs and student debt have Americans doubting the value of higher education, there's growing interest in high-paying jobs that don't require a de...
articles.body:
As college costs and student debt have Americans doubting the value of higher education, there's growing interest in high-paying jobs that don't require a degree - and in public policy supporting training for them. But six-figure jobs that skip a bachelor's degree do require more than a high school diploma and remain rare, according to an analysis released Monday by Niche, a higher education platform.

The highest salaries for workers without a bachelor's degree are typically in jobs gated by federal certification or specialized training, including commercial pilots, air traffic controllers, elevator installers and nuclear reactor operators, the study shows.

The findings counter an emerging narrative about the prevalence of six-figure jobs in the skilled trades that don't require higher education. Politicians and business leaders have touted careers in electrical work, HVAC and plumbing earning more than $100,000, arguing that a four-year degree is unnecessary for financial security.

While those jobs offer healthy salaries, research shows their median earnings are more modest than salaries for less common occupations that don't require a bachelor's degree.

Using data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Niche economist Allison Shrivastava found that only 9.4 percent of occupations with a median wage of $100,000 or more don't require a bachelor's degree. Those occupations account for just 0.3 percent of 13.8 million annual openings projected across every occupation in which a bachelor's is not a prerequisite.

There are four times as many openings that do not require a bachelor's degree, but the jobs generally pay less. On average, the median earnings for those occupations are around $45,000 a year, compared with $96,000 for job openings seeking people with a bachelor's degree, according to the analysis.

"There's a little bit of romanticizing the trades," Shrivastava said. "There are some trade jobs that you can make six figures right out the gate, but they are more the exception than the rule."

She said that doesn't discount the power vocational training has to lift people out of poverty and provide economic success. But those workers have less earning potential than people with a bachelor's degree, and can have a harder time finding work in other fields without additional training, Shrivastava said.

A study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research found the college wage premium - the extra pay degree holders make compared to workers with only a high school diploma - doubles over a worker's lifetime, from 27 percent at age 25 to 60 percent at age 55. Workers with college degrees obtain jobs in professions with greater scope for on-the-job training and wage growth, according to the study.

articles.title: FAA halts flights in Northeast after fiber cable cut in NJ
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted flights at multiple airports in the Northeast on Monday, citing the accidental cutting of a fiber cable at a construction site in New Jersey. Ground stops were originally in effect at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in Queens, N.Y.; Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR); Philadelphia International Airport (PHL);…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted flights at multiple airports in the Northeast on Monday, citing the accidental cutting of a fiber cable at a construction site in New Jersey.

Ground stops were originally in effect at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in Queens, N.Y.; Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR); Philadelphia International Airport (PHL); and Teterboro Airport (TEB) in New Jersey, according to the FAA’s National Airspace System Status page.

Ground delays, meanwhile, were in effect at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) in Queens, Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and PHL. Flights departing LGA, BOS and PHL were delayed by an average of 44 minutes, 105 minutes and 212 minutes, respectively.

Bryan Bedford, the administrator of the FAA, said Monday the 600-foot fiber cable cut occurred “somewhere between” New Brunswick and Newark, N.J.

“Somebody dug it up,” Bedford told reporters, as captured on video by CBS News’s Kris Van Cleave. The FAA administrator later said the fiber cable was cut earlier Monday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew accidentally cut into the fiber line, causing a “telecom outage” and the subsequent flight disruptions. Duffy noted flights would resume out of LGA and PHL but remain paused out of EWR, JFK and TEB.

“This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future,” Duffy wrote on social media Monday.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, — which President Trump signed into law last year — provided the FAA with $12.5 billion to modernize the national air traffic control system. Officials from the aviation agency have asked for an additional $10 billion from Congress to upgrade the air traffic control system.

The ground stops and delays at New York City-area airports are in effect as world leaders, including Trump, are descending on the Big Apple for the United Nations General Assembly this week.

The stoppages and delays have placed a strain on other airports in the region. Later Monday afternoon, the FAA imposed a ground stop at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) until at least 4 p.m. EDT.

At EWR, roughly 1 in 3 departing flights were canceled, according to data from FlightAware. Another 96 flights scheduled to leave Newark were delayed, accounting for 17 percent of departures, per FlightAware.

articles.title: Collins, Murray speak out against reported Trump push to ‘politicize grantmaking’
articles.summary: Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Patty Murray (D-Wash.), leaders of the Senate Appropriations Committee, spoke out Monday against the White House’s reported plans to give political appointees more control over the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) grantmaking process. Multiple outlets reported over the weekend that the White House is planning to impose more political oversight…
articles.body:
Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Patty Murray (D-Wash.), leaders of the Senate Appropriations Committee, spoke out Monday against the White House’s reported plans to give political appointees more control over the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) grantmaking process.

Multiple outlets reported over the weekend that the White House is planning to impose more political oversight over NIH grantmaking due to the administration’s belief that the agency is rewarding research that goes against President Trump’s agenda.

White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought has reportedly accused the NIH of funding “woke” initiatives, though NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya is said to have defended his agency’s grantmaking process.

Collins, chair of the Senate Appropriations panel, denounced the OMB’s potential involvement in how NIH grants are awarded.

“The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) should not be involved in agency decisions on the awards of grants. As I stated in my July 6 letter, a proposed OMB rule would politicize grantmaking. The Continuing Resolution — which passed the Senate, House, and was signed into law on September 2 — blocks OMB’s proposed rule or any substantially similar one,” Collins said in a statement.

“Any attempt to politicize grantmaking at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), or any other agency, by another means—whether an Executive Order or guidance—is contrary to congressional intent,” added Collins. “Imposing a political review on awards that have already been selected through a rigorous scientific and merit-based process undermines the long-standing principle that the government funds awards based on scientific need and merit, rather than political ideology.”

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Murray, ranking member of the Appropriations Committee, said NIH grants should not be decided by a “panel of lackeys chosen by Donald Trump and Russ Vought.”

“Only one question should decide which research gets funded: is this good science that could save lives? Trump wants to answer a different question: does this help me settle a score? NIH funding doesn’t belong to Donald Trump — it belongs to the patients and families waiting on the next medical breakthrough,” she said in a statement.

“President Trump will stop at nothing to defund medical research that fundamentally changes the lives of patients and families across the country, and Republicans need to join us to put a stop to any effort by this administration to politicize what groundbreaking new treatments and cures we decide as a country to invest in — whether that’s an OMB rule or a new executive order,” Murray added.

The White House has yet to publicly confirm the reported plans, and an executive order like the one reported by The New York Times that would give an external committee authority to veto grants has not yet been issued as of Monday afternoon.

articles.title: Homem no para-choque de caminhão em Ribeirão e o risco de multa | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo advogado especialista em trânsito, a infração ocorre mesmo que o condutor não perceba a pessoa na parte externa do veículo. RP Mobi diz que não recebeu informações sobre o homem nem sobre o motorista.
articles.summary: Flagrante de homem no para-choque de caminhão em Ribeirão Preto alerta para multa grave, aplicada mesmo que o motorista não saiba da presença do passageiro.
articles.body:
Um homem foi filmado deitado no para-choque traseiro de um caminhão em movimento na manhã desta terça-feira (22), na Estrada Antônia Mugnatto Marincek, em Ribeirão Preto (SP). Segundo um advogado especialista em trânsito, o motorista pode ser multado mesmo que não saiba que levava alguém do lado de fora do veículo.

As imagens foram feitas pela telespectadora Talita Barbosa, que seguia para o trabalho, e enviadas à EPTV, afiliada da TV Globo. O flagrante foi registrado na altura do Jardim Florestan Fernandes. No vídeo, o homem aparece deitado sobre sacos de lixo, apoiado na traseira do caminhão.

Talita contou que não foi a primeira vez que viu o homem na mesma situação. Ela disse não saber se o motorista sabia do passageiro nem para onde o caminhão seguiu.

Nem o homem nem o motorista foram identificados. Procurada pela EPTV , a RP Mobi, empresa responsável pelo trânsito em Ribeirão Preto, afirmou que a situação é inadequada e contraria o Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB). A empresa disse que não recebeu informações sobre o estado do homem nem sobre o motorista.

Homem viaja deitado em para-choque trazeiro de caminhão — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

De acordo com o advogado Rodrigo Paschoalotto, a infração acontece pelo simples fato de haver uma pessoa na parte externa do veículo, tenha o motorista percebido ou não.

O artigo 235 do CTB proíbe conduzir pessoas, animais ou carga nas partes externas do veículo, salvo quando houver autorização. A infração é grave e prevê multa de R$ 195,23, cinco pontos na Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH) e retenção do veículo até que a pessoa seja retirada.

Se a situação for flagrada por um agente de trânsito, o motorista pode ser autuado. Ainda segundo o advogado, se ficar comprovado que ele sabia que havia alguém no para-choque, pode ser responsabilizado criminalmente caso a pessoa caia e morra.

Rodrigo orienta que o motorista avisado de que há alguém na parte externa do caminhão pare o veículo imediatamente e peça que a pessoa desça. Se ela se recusar, a orientação é acionar a polícia.

"Ele tem que parar o veículo imediatamente. Ele não pode mais percorrer com esse veículo nem mais um metro", afirmou.

articles.title: Macaé reforça apreensão de animais de grande porte soltos nas ruas | G1
articles.standfirst: Serviço permanente recolhe bichos em vias públicas para evitar acidentes e destina para adoção os casos de abandono ou maus-tratos.
articles.summary: Serviço permanente recolhe bichos em vias públicas para evitar acidentes e destina para adoção os casos de abandono ou maus-tratos.
articles.body:
Equipes especializadas realizam o recolhimento e garantem exames e abrigo para os bichos — Foto: Arquivo Secom

A Prefeitura de Macaé realiza um trabalho contínuo de fiscalização e recolhimento de animais de grande porte encontrados soltos ou amarrados em vias públicas. A medida, amparada por legislação municipal, visa prevenir acidentes no trânsito urbano e garantir o bem-estar dos próprios bichos, combatendo situações de abandono e maustratos pela cidade.

O serviço conta com um caminhão adaptado e profissionais especializados para o manejo seguro dos animais. Após o recolhimento — motivado por rondas ou denúncias recebidas pela Ouvidoria e pelo WhatsApp (22) 99285-6779 —, os equinos são encaminhados para um centro de apreensão, onde passam por avaliação veterinária e recebem os cuidados necessários.

Legislação do município prevê multas para tutores e impede a devolução em casos de maus-tratos — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Para reaver o animal, o proprietário deve se apresentar em até sete dias, comprovar a posse e quitar as taxas e multas previstas no Código de Posturas e em leis municipais. A legislação proíbe amarrar bichos em postes, árvores e grades. Caso o prazo expire sem procura ou fique comprovada a prática de maus-tratos, o antigo tutor perde o direito ao resgate, e o animal é direcionado para adoção responsável com acompanhamento da Secretaria.

Desde o início das operações, 36 cavalos foram recolhidos das ruas do município. Destes, seis foram reavidos por seus tutores mediante regularização e nove já ganharam novos lares por meio da adoção qualificada, enquanto os demais permanecem abrigados aguardando a finalização dos trâmites legais.

articles.title: UN panel calls for guardrails on AI as current safeguards are ‘unraveling’
articles.summary: The United Nations-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI on Monday urged world leaders and tech companies to implement new safeguards on artificial intelligence, with the concern that existing safeguards are “unraveling.” U.N. Secretary General António Gueterres welcomed the report and encouraged “external experts, including from frontier AI labs and AI safety institutes, to engage…
articles.body:
The United Nations-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI on Monday urged world leaders and tech companies to implement new safeguards on artificial intelligence, with the concern that existing safeguards are “unraveling.”

U.N. Secretary General António Gueterres welcomed the report and encouraged “external experts, including from frontier AI labs and AI safety institutes, to engage with the panel to help inform dialogue on such matters.”

“This is not only a question of speed,” the panel’s experts said in a report released by UN News. “It leaves open whether safeguards designed today will work once agents can understand them and plan around them. In simple terms, the traditional model of safeguarding is unravelling.”

The panel released a brief called “AI Agents, Misalignment and Loss of Human Control Risks: Evidence from the OpenAI-Hugging Face Incident.” The document details how the hack carried out by “AI agents” during a test run by OpenAI on the online platform Hugging Face occurred after a security breach.

OpenAI stated in July that two of its models, including its latest GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model, breached past network restrictions and broke into Hugging Face’s database without any prompt to do so. This compromised parts of OpenAI’s and Hugging Face’s systems.

Panelists said this incident raises “fears that humans will one day no longer be able to steer, constrain or stop AI,” noting that in their report that it was “an early warning of one possible route to more severe future loss of control.”

“Researchers have long warned that three conditions could lead to loss of control: a misaligned goal, the capability to pursue it and an environment that allows it,” panel co-chair Yoshua Bengio told UN News. “This summer, all three came together in a real system, not a laboratory. Since this is not an isolated observation of misaligned goals, this raises serious questions about the way AI agents are currently trained.”

The report stated that existing approaches, including human authority over “high-hazard systems” and plans to address failure, can manage major risks. But panelists said that none of these and proposed “instruments guarantee safety.”

“Although the probability of loss of control events remains uncertain and the best response is still under debate, a clear conclusion emerges: given the severity of these events, risk management requires far greater attention and resources,” the report’s conclusion reads.

Concerns over AI and AI development have risen among lawmakers and other elected officials on both sides of the aisle in recent weeks. Many have called for strong regulations on the emerging technology, while others have urged that development slow down to allow lawmakers to pass legislative proposals.

These concerns were raised after Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both Anthropic and OpenAI, warned earlier this month that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Some have dismissed Coxon’s “doomsday” warning. President Trump on Saturday announced that he will have an “AI Force” and an “AI czar” to oversee the technology’s development, but he denounced fears of the technology’s potential risks as a “hoax.”

articles.title: China, EU Should Avoid Trade Clash, Beijing’s Top Diplomat Says
articles.summary: China and the EU should find a way to avoid a confrontation over trade, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said — comments that come as a deadline to find solutions to...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- China and the EU should find a way to avoid a confrontation over trade, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said — comments that come as a deadline to find solutions to the two sides' differences approaches.

"China and the European Union are comprehensive strategic partners, and a trade war should not be fought between them," Wang said in a call with German counterpart Johann Wadephul, according to a statement from Beijing late Monday.

Wang said he hoped Germany would "maintain a rational and pragmatic attitude," and encourage Brussels to "stay on the right track of open cooperation, dialogue and consultation."

The comments underscore mounting concern that China and Europe are heading toward a clash. For Beijing, the timing wouldn't be ideal considering it has similar friction with Washington. Chinese leader Xi Jinping is heading to the US this week to try to negotiate an extension to a trade war ceasefire with President Donald Trump.

EU leaders are set to meet in the middle of next month to discuss the trade deficit with China and possible new instruments they can use to strike back against Beijing's trade practices. Beijing and Brussels earlier agreed to set an October deadline to make progress on trade disagreements.

Earlier this month, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic held a call with Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao to discuss the management of exports to the EU, European access to China's market and export controls of rare earths.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has also warned that the bloc's trade deficit with China has reached a tipping point.

"Let me be clear: we will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship," she said in her state of the union address earlier this month. "Words are good. But deeds are better."

articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu to engineers: Use AI but never ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has warned engineers against relying too heavily on artificial intelligence for software development. In an X post, Sridhar.
articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has warned engineers against relying too heavily on artificial intelligence for software development. In an X post, Sridhar Vembu said that engineers should use AI tools without giving up their own understanding of the work. Vembu was responding to a post by a software engineer who described the use of Anthropic's Claude Code at a large company. The engineer claimed that AI was being used to create almost every part of the software development process, including specifications, code, tests, product requirement documents (PRDs), tickets and reports."Nobody knows anything here. The specs, code, tests, PRDs, tickets, resolution of those tickets, reports, etc., everything is made by Claude Code. Nobody on my team likes this. They are being forced to ship as much as they can," the engineer wrote.Sridhar Vembu quoted and replied “This is sad. I tell our engineers to use AI but never cede our understanding to AI”. He also warned that companies may be adopting AI-powered coding tools faster than engineers can understand their impact.“As an industry, we are driving too fast in a fancy new car we barely understand how to drive, inviting disaster,” Vembu stated.Engineer says AI is changing software developmentThe engineer's post also raised concerns about the pressure to deliver more code as AI makes software development faster. According to the post, employees were working 12 to 13 hours a day while spending much of their time directing AI tools instead of writing or understanding code themselves. The engineer said there was little time to inspect what the AI had produced or understand how different parts of the system worked.“People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter,” the engineer wrote.“There is no sense of victory. Nobody is resolving bugs. In reality, nobody is thinking anymore. Everything is done by LLMs. It is so soul-sucking. I would not mind it, to be honest, if we were at least given the time to check out the code and see what is going where. But no, the goal is to just ship. No matter what happens,” the engineer wrote.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says ‘nothing would give me more joy’ than to pay more taxes: ‘I'm just afraid of being poor’
articles.summary: While California faces a billionaire exodus ahead of the November 3 wealth tax vote, Huang has taken a much different stance.
articles.body:
While California faces a billionaire exodus ahead of its November 3 wealth tax vote, Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang says he'd happily pay more to the tax man.

During a recent interview with CBS News , Huang — whose net worth Forbes recently pegged at more than $197 billion — was asked about the prospect of having to pay up to $8 billion in taxes over five years if Proposition 40 passes. He responded that "it's a privilege, it's a responsibility" to pay taxes and that "nothing would give me more joy" than to pay more.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

"The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," the 63-year-old explained. "The more you make, the more taxes you pay. So, I'm okay with that."

Proposition 40 — a one-off wealth tax on 5% of the net worth of any billionaire living in the state as of January 1 of this year — would, in theory, generate billions of dollars primarily for public healthcare services but also for education and food assistance programs. It's estimated that California is currently home to around 260 billionaires — the most of any state — and that the tax could raise more than $108 billion in revenue. California also has the highest combined federal and state income tax rate, which tops out at 50.3% .

Neither Huang or Nvidia replied to Moneywise's request for comment, but the billionaire told CBS that he's "not afraid of paying taxes." Rather, he quipped that he harbors a different concern: "I'm just afraid of being poor."

From Denny's dishwasher to tech billionaire

At first, a billionaire expressing concern about becoming poor could come off as somewhat tone deaf. In the second quarter of 2026, for example, the median weekly earnings for full-time U.S. wage and salary workers hit $1,258 — or roughly $67,500 if calculated across the entire year. Meanwhile, a 2026 SEC filing put Huang's 2026 compensation at above $36 million .

But Huang wasn't born into privilege. Originally from Taiwan, he was sent by his parents , along with his older brother, to the U.S. at age nine to live with an uncle in the hopes of achieving a better life.

articles.title: Hung Cao’s bid for Navy secretary faces choppy waters post-USS Abraham Lincoln
articles.summary: President Trump’s official nomination of Hung Cao to be Navy secretary is already in jeopardy after Democratic senators indicated they won’t vote in favor of giving him the waiver needed to serve. Cao, a Trump loyalist who has served as the acting head of the Navy since April and was officially nominated on Sept. 1,…
articles.body:
President Trump’s official nomination of Hung Cao to be Navy secretary is already in jeopardy after Democratic senators indicated they won’t vote in favor of giving him the waiver needed to serve.

Cao, a Trump loyalist who has served as the acting head of the Navy since April and was officially nominated on Sept. 1, will need 60 votes in the Senate for a waiver given his previous stint in the service, where he retired as a captain in 2021. Federal law requires former military officers to wait seven to 10 years before they can take several top civilian roles at the Pentagon.

But Democrats told The Hill they have serious concerns with Cao’s track record while serving as the Navy’s top civilian, including the handling of the troubled USS Abraham Lincoln deployment, which stretched roughly nine months as it supported the U.S. war in Iran.

“Hung Cao has shown he has neither the ability nor the temperament to serve as Navy Secretary,” Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) said in a statement to The Hill.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) said beyond the logistical hurdles with getting Cao confirmed “due to the Trump administration’s botched nomination requiring a waiver,” she expects he will have to answer to what she called a “severe mishandling” of the Lincoln’s deployment to the Middle East that led to deteriorating mental health issues onboard.

She added that after speaking to Cao at a recent Senate Armed Services Committee hearing, she has some outstanding questions regarding funding and workforce concerns at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, which is located in Maine but borders New Hampshire. The shipyard helps maintain the country’s nuclear-attack submarines.

Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), said she has concerns about Cao’s “ability to preserve the integrity and safety of the Navy” as it faces “dire readiness concerns, depleted munitions stockpiles, and distractions from pacing challenges in the Indo-Pacific.”

“Our Navy needs steady, experienced leadership that will prioritize our national security and the safety of our servicemembers above all else,” Hirono said in a statement to The Hill. “Given Acting Secretary Cao’s lack of leadership in addressing the concerns raised regarding the extended deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln and his focus on advancing Secretary Hegseth’s ideological war on DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion], I have concerns about Mr. Cao’s ability to preserve the integrity and safety of the Navy.”

She added that she is looking to see if Cao “is prepared to uphold his oath to protect the Constitution and our country.”

Cao — who since April has been serving as acting Navy secretary since John Phelan unexpectedly left the role — spent 25 years in the service as a special operations officer with deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia. After he retired, he twice ran for office unsuccessfully in Virginia, one for a House seat in 2022 and then for a Senate seat in 2024.

In February 2025 Trump nominated Cao as undersecretary of the Navy. He was narrowly confirmed by the Senate in a 52-45 vote in October of that year.

It’s not unthinkable for a former service member to receive a waiver from Congress to serve at the Pentagon. Lawmakers granted one to retired Marine Corps Gen. Jim Mattis to become Defense secretary in Trump’s first term and one to retired Army Gen. Lloyd Austin for the same position under former President Biden.

But Trump, who praised Cao as “a true WARRIOR” in announcing his nomination, has a difficult candidate in terms of his political baggage.

While running for Senate in 2024, Cao said the military needs “alpha males and alpha females who are going to rip out their own guts, eat them, and ask for seconds.”

After Trump announced Cao’s nomination, Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) referred to those comments in a post to social media , saying, “This is not a serious person who should be leading our servicemembers, especially during a war.”

The acting secretary also came under intense scrutiny for his handling of the Lincoln deployment, which left its California home port in November 2025 and was beset by reports of poor living conditions and deteriorating mental health among sailors after the ship was sent to the Middle East in January.

Cao in August acknowledged the stresses being faced by the crew but insisted the U.S. military’s mission “demanded” the Lincoln’s deployment be extended past the initial end date in May, calling the media coverage of it “dishonest.”

Keeping Cao as the nominee also opens the Navy to more intense scrutiny amid numerous bipartisan concerns. Those include a strained Navy budget and fleet due to the Iran war; mounting mental health issues among service members; Trump’s intended “Golden Fleet” which will include new, heavily armed Navy ships named after himself; and the president’s recent directive to install old steam-powered technology on U.S. aircraft carriers, a costly endeavor.

Confirmation votes are generally just the purview of the Senate.

Cao’s need for a waiver from Congress also means the House will weigh in on the exemption with hearings and floor votes in both chambers.

Those votes, if they happen, are unlikely to take place until after the November midterm elections as the House and Senate are only in Washington for two more weeks before then.

articles.title: Beyer calls on FAA to suspend AI system for DC-area airports: ‘Guinea pigs’
articles.summary: A top Democrat is calling on the Trump administration to halt the implementation of a new artificial intelligence (AI) system designed to streamline air travel. Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) warned that the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) new AI tool, which aims to eliminate flight delays and cancellations, is being launched without assurances of public safety.…
articles.body:
A top Democrat is calling on the Trump administration to halt the implementation of a new artificial intelligence (AI) system designed to streamline air travel.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) warned that the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) new AI tool, which aims to eliminate flight delays and cancellations, is being launched without assurances of public safety.

“The FAA should not use my constituents as guinea pigs for an unproven AI air traffic control system,” Beyer said Monday in a statement . “The safety of the 24 million people traveling through DCA each year must be the top priority.”

The warning echoes the broader concerns on Capitol Hill surrounding the development and implementation of AI, particularly after several leading industry voices sounded alarms this month about the potentially existential dangers the rapidly growing technology poses to humans.

The new FAA tool, dubbed the Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories (“SMART”) system, is designed to crunch a host of factors — including weather patterns, airport capacity and real-time airspace conditions — to help manage air traffic and ease congestion at the nation’s airports.

The system launched on Monday at three airports around the nation’s capital — Reagan Washington National (DCA), Dulles International (IAD) and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall (BWI) — with future plans to expand nationwide.

“By fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace and preventing problems before they happen, SMART will slash those frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote Monday in a statement.

Beyer is skeptical. The six-term House veteran is a co-chair of the Congressional AI Caucus, a bipartisan group that seeks to advise fellow policymakers on the emerging technology. And he also represents the Northern Virginia district that’s home to DCA.

The Democratic lawmaker said he was informed Monday that air traffic controllers had no hand in the design of the SMART system, nor have they been trained in its use.

“I was further informed that the air traffic controllers have been told the ‘SMART’ system can adjust schedules and potentially even routes,” he continued. “Despite outward appearances, the airlines reportedly were privately ‘panicking’ about the hasty implementation of this system.”

Beyer is urging the FAA to suspend the rollout of the tool until it can be vetted more thoroughly by human operators on the ground — “at the very least until it is clearly established beyond doubt via air traffic controller feedback and independently verified stress testing that the technology is safe.”

“Dangerously rushing a system that holds Americans’ lives in its hands is not a good use case for artificial intelligence,” he said.

articles.title: What Xi Jinping wants from his summit with Donald Trump
articles.summary: When Xi Jinping arrives in Washington this week for his first visit to the US capital in 11 years, China's leader is expected to focus on five...
articles.body:
When Xi Jinping arrives in Washington this week for his first visit to the US capital in 11 years, China's leader is expected to focus on five areas in his talks with President Donald Trump.

Xi's most urgent goal will be to extend a trade truce that the two leaders sealed in the South Korean city of Busan last October after a brief but fierce tariff war, Chinese scholars and analysts say.

China's leader is also expected to discuss AI safety and how to end the Iran war, as well as agreements to buy US soyabeans or Boeing aircraft. And Xi is set to push hard against Washington's support for Taiwan, over which Beijing claims sovereignty.

But his most important aim will be to preserve the détente between China and the US that the two sides described as "constructive strategic stability" when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing in May. In the relative diplomatic quiet since then, China has accelerated efforts to upgrade the nation's technology to compete with the US and revive a domestic economy that is suffering from a five-year property bust.

"'Stable' by itself already means 'constructive'," said an international relations scholar in Beijing. "Because in 2024 and 2025, we did not expect that there would be stability between China and the United States."

The number one goal for Xi will be to extend the Busan truce . China's global trade surplus, which helped spark a trade war during Trump's first term, is on track to exceed 2025's record $1.2tn, even though its direct exports to the US have fallen in recent years.

After Busan, the US cut tariffs on China, but the agreement is set to expire on November 10. If the truce is not extended, the two sides could reimpose higher tariffs and stringent export controls that were frozen last year.

Senior US and Chinese officials discussed extending the truce at the weekend but did not reach agreement, according to people familiar with the talks.

Washington believes China has not sufficiently lived up to its promise to ease export controls on rare earths critical to high-tech manufacturing and is threatening to extend the truce for only six months. China wants it to run until the end of Trump's term.

China has previously agreed to buy 25mn tonnes of soyabeans and an additional $17bn of other US agricultural products annually.

There is speculation Xi will bring a delegation of high-powered Chinese business leaders to Washington. That would mirror Trump's entourage in Beijing in May, which included Apple's Tim Cook, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Tesla's Elon Musk.

articles.title: Meta patches Muse exploit that let attackers control the AI agent
articles.summary: Meta has issued a patch for its Muse macOS app following the discovery of a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of the AI agent.
articles.body: Meta has issued a patch for its Muse macOS app following the discovery of a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of the AI agent. The bug found by security researcher Patrick Wardle utilized an undocumented Muse setting that enabled potential attackers running local code to redirect transcription processing from Meta’s servers to their own endpoint, Ars Technica reports, giving the attacker access to the Muse account. Several design decisions reportedly enabled this flaw, including having Muse dictation occur in the cloud instead of on-device, and allowing any app to control all of Muse’s undocumented settings. Proof-of-concept attacks developed by Wardle to test the exploit enabled him to take pictures and write malicious files to disk via Muse, which did not alert the user in many cases. “We can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want. So instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself,” Wardle told Ars Technica. “At the very least, they should be thinking about security from the very start, and they are just not.” That stands in contrast with the emphasis that Meta placed on Muse’s privacy and security features when it announced the AI agent earlier this month. Meta patched the vulnerability in the hours following the Ars report being published, and asserts that real-world security concerns were minimal because the exploit required local access to the user’s device. “This was a local privilege escalation attack, not a remote exploit. Using it to do harm therefore requires malicious code already running on the user’s machine under their user account and the practical risk to users of the Muse Mac app was therefore quite low,” David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs said on X. “Nonetheless, we have issued a hotfix to the app to address the issue.” While quickly addressed, the Muse exploit comes at a time when Meta’s AI agent is already being scrutinized as the company tries to claw back ground from rival AI providers. Amazon recently blocked Muse from accessing its e-commerce platform and claims Meta never obtained its permission to do so. Still, the launch has been successful for Meta — during its first 12 days, estimated downloads of the Muse mobile app have reportedly outpaced ChatGPT’s own 12-day debut in the US and Canada, with Meta stock climbing by 11 percent on Monday.

articles.title: AI malware can rewrite itself to evade detection
articles.summary: Google's Threat Intelligence Group found PROMPTFLUX malware that uses Gemini to rewrite its own code every hour, raising urgent cybersecurity alarms.
articles.body: Google's Threat Intelligence Group found experimental malware called PROMPTFLUX that could ask Gemini to rewrite its own code. One version was designed to do that every hour. Why would malware keep rewriting itself? To make it harder to recognize. Security software can look for known patterns in malicious code. If that code keeps changing, the malware becomes a moving target. That does not automatically make it invisible to current security tools, but it can make some types of detection more difficult. There is an important reality check here. PROMPTFLUX was still being developed when Google found it. Researchers had yet to see it successfully compromise a victim's device or network, and Google disabled assets connected to the activity. What caught my attention is what came next. Google has since documented AI being used by malware during live attacks. It has also uncovered an Android backdoor that can use AI to understand what is happening on a phone and help decide what to do next. That tells us where this could be heading. So let’s break down how AI-powered malware works and what you can do to protect yourself. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com How PROMPTFLUX used AI to rewrite itself PROMPTFLUX was a VBScript-based malware project that Google discovered in June 2025. Its most interesting component was called the "Thinking Robot." The malware could contact Gemini and request new obfuscation techniques designed to make its code harder for security software to recognize. Google later found multiple PROMPTFLUX variations. One included instructions telling Gemini to rewrite the malware’s entire source code every hour while preserving the pieces needed for it to continue working. Think about what that means from the defender’s side. Security software may identify one version of malicious code. Then the program can generate a different-looking version while continuing to pursue the same goal. That creates a moving target. Google described PROMPTFLUX as an early example of "just-in-time" AI being built directly into malware. Instead of relying entirely on functions written ahead of time, malware can ask an AI model for help while it runs. Does rewriting malware make antivirus useless? No, and this is where I want to be careful. You may hear AI malware described as something that can simply change its appearance and walk right past antivirus protection. The reality has more layers. Signature detection still plays a role in cybersecurity. Security software can recognize the digital fingerprints of known malware and block them quickly. However, antivirus protection does much more than compare a file with a list of known threats. Microsoft Defender Antivirus, for example, uses real-time monitoring, behavioral analysis and heuristic protection. It also uses cloud-delivered protection and machine learning to help identify new threats that may not match a known malware signature. That means changing the code does not automatically make malware invisible. A security tool may still notice suspicious behavior once the malware starts doing something dangerous. PROMPTFLUX is concerning because it can make one form of detection harder. That does not mean every layer of modern antivirus suddenly stops working. PROMPTSTEAL brought AI-powered malware into live attacks PROMPTFLUX was experimental. PROMPTSTEAL crossed an important line. Google identified the Russian government-backed group APT28 using PROMPTSTEAL against targets in Ukraine. Google says this was its first observation of malware querying a large language model while deployed in live operations. PROMPTSTEAL takes a different approach from PROMPTFLUX. Instead of asking AI to rewrite itself, it queries the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model through Hugging Face. The model generates Windows commands that PROMPTSTEAL can execute. Those commands can gather information about a computer and copy documents from folders including Documents, Downloads and Desktop. The malware then sends collected information back to infrastructure controlled by the attacker. That is a significant change. The AI model becomes part of what the malware does after it starts running. PROMPTSPY shows how AI malware could react to your phone Then came PROMPTSPY. Google detailed the Android backdoor in May 2026 after it was initially identified by ESET. PROMPTSPY contains an AI-powered module called GeminiAutomationAgent. It can send information about what appears on an infected Android device to Gemini and use the response to help navigate the phone’s interface. In other words, the malware can use AI to understand part of what is happening on the screen and determine how to interact with it. Google found that PROMPTSPY could also make itself harder to remove. When a victim tried to uninstall it, the malware could place an invisible overlay over the uninstall button so taps would appear to do nothing. There is some good news for Android users. Google says it took action against the actor behind the malware. It also said no apps containing PROMPTSPY were found on Google Play at the time of its May report. Known versions are detected by Google Play Protect, which is enabled by default on Android devices with Google Play Services. Still, PROMPTSPY gives us a much clearer picture of where this technology could go. Malware can begin reacting to the device it finds instead of relying only on instructions written before the attack starts. HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER Google’s latest report shows attackers want more automation Google’s newest report makes the larger trend harder to ignore. On Sept. 8, 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group said it had seen attackers move from basic AI prompting toward agentic AI workflows and AI-enabled automation. That means AI can start taking on larger pieces of an operation with less human involvement. One example really jumped out at me. Google says a suspected financially motivated attacker compromised a company’s cloud infrastructure. The attacker then used an AI coding chatbot and agent instructions to plan, build and execute a mass credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours. The system could manage vulnerability scanning and troubleshoot problems while the attack was underway. Google says thousands of third-party credentials were compromised. Google has also seen attackers experimenting with automated reconnaissance and frameworks designed to manage harvested credentials. However, there is another important reality check. Google says it has yet to observe threat actors deploying fully autonomous exploit pipelines against targets in the wild. We have not reached the point where an AI system independently launches every part of a cyberattack without people involved. The amount of work AI can take off an attacker’s hands keeps growing, though. Security teams already face an enormous amount of malware AI arrives on top of an already huge malware problem. Independent security institute AV-TEST says it registers more than 450,000 new malicious programs and potentially unwanted applications every day. That number does not mean 450,000 completely different attacks are hitting people every day. Malware samples can include different versions and variations of existing threats. Still, the volume shows why security companies cannot depend on recognizing every malicious file by its appearance alone. Meanwhile, the financial damage tied to cyber-enabled crime continues to climb. The FBI says Americans reported nearly $21 billion in cyber-enabled crime losses during 2025, up 26% from the year before. Those losses cover many kinds of online crime and cannot be attributed to AI malware. However, they show what criminals already stand to gain when technology makes attacks easier to run. 9 ways to protect yourself as malware gets smarter You do not need to understand how an AI model rewrites VBScript to protect yourself. The best defense still comes from making it harder for malware to reach your device and harder for it to succeed if something slips through. 1) Use antivirus protection that watches behavior Look for strong antivirus software with real-time protection and behavioral detection. That becomes especially useful when malicious software changes enough that a traditional signature may not recognize it immediately. The right protection can watch what a program does after it starts running. Suspicious file changes or attempts to alter sensitive system settings can trigger another layer of detection. If you are comparing protection, see our guide to what to look for in antivirus software without the jargon. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 2) Keep real-time and cloud protection turned on Security software cannot help as much if its strongest protections have been disabled. On Windows, Microsoft says Defender’s behavior monitoring is enabled by default. Cloud-delivered protection also helps detect new and emerging threats. If a website, pop-up or random tutorial tells you to disable antivirus protection so something will install, stop. Do not turn off security protections to make a questionable download work. 3) Turn on automatic software updates Keep your operating system and browser current. Do the same for software you use regularly. Attackers often look for people running software with vulnerabilities that already have patches available. Automatic updates can close those openings without forcing you to track every security bulletin yourself. CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN 4) Never paste a computer command because a website tells you to This has become one of the most important malware warnings I can give you. Attackers increasingly use fake CAPTCHA pages and bogus error messages to tell victims to open Windows Run, PowerShell, Command Prompt or Terminal. The page then asks them to paste a command. Do not do it. A legitimate CAPTCHA should never require you to run a command on your computer. We recently reported that more than 5,400 compromised websites were being used in one campaign built around this trick. See how thousands of hacked sites can trick you into installing malware. 5) Pay attention when your browser or computer warns you Security warnings can feel annoying when you are trying to download something quickly. Do not automatically click past them. Microsoft Defender SmartScreen, for example, can check websites and downloads for signs of phishing or malicious software. If your browser blocks a file or tells you a site looks dangerous, investigate before continuing. A website should never pressure you to weaken your computer’s security so you can proceed. 6) Be careful where you get apps and browser extensions PROMPTSPY gives Android users a good reason to pay attention to where apps come from. Google says Play Protect checks apps for harmful behavior. It also scans apps installed from outside Google Play. Keep Play Protect enabled. Be especially cautious with sideloaded apps from websites, messages or unfamiliar app stores. The same thinking applies to browser extensions. An extension can gain significant access to what happens inside your browser, so install only what you need from a source you trust. 7) Use a password manager and stronger account protection A password manager helps you create unique passwords for your accounts. It can also give you a useful phishing warning. If a saved password normally fills automatically and suddenly does not, stop and check the website address before typing the password yourself. Use multifactor authentication where available. Better yet, use a passkey when a service supports one. Keep in mind that some information-stealing malware can target browser cookies or authenticated sessions. MFA still helps, but no login protection gives you permission to ignore malware on the device itself. 8) Keep a separate backup of important files Back up anything you would hate to lose. That could include family photos and financial records. Keep other irreplaceable files covered too. A cloud backup can help. An external drive that you disconnect when you are finished backing up can give you another recovery option. A backup will not stop malware from stealing data, but it can make ransomware or destructive malware much less devastating. 9) Know what to do if you think malware got through Watch for unfamiliar programs and unexplained security alerts. Pay attention if your antivirus suddenly turns itself off or your browser starts behaving strangely. If you think a computer may be infected, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan. For a PC, you can follow our guide on what to do if you think your PC has a virus. If passwords or financial information may have been exposed, use a different trusted device to change important passwords. Then sign out of active sessions where the service allows it. Check your financial accounts for activity you do not recognize. Act quickly if something looks wrong. Kurt’s key takeaways PROMPTFLUX caught my attention because of what it says about the direction malware is taking. For years, attackers have found ways to change malicious code and make detection harder. AI gives them another tool for doing that while the malware is running. I would not take that to mean antivirus protection suddenly became obsolete. Strong security software already looks beyond a simple malware fingerprint. Behavior monitoring and cloud-based analysis can help catch threats that have never been seen before. What concerns me more is how quickly the technology is progressing. PROMPTFLUX was experimental. PROMPTSTEAL appeared in live operations. PROMPTSPY showed how AI could help malware interpret an Android interface. Now Google is seeing attackers use agentic AI to automate larger portions of an attack. For me, the lesson is pretty straightforward. Do not depend on one security feature to save you. Keep good protection running, take security warnings seriously and make it difficult for malicious software to get onto your devices in the first place. If something does get through, reacting quickly can limit how far the damage goes. As malware becomes capable of changing its code and making more decisions with AI, do you think security companies can stay ahead, or are we heading toward a point where it becomes much harder to know whether our devices are truly safe? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Report CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Airports resume operations after massive disruptions in Northeast
articles.summary: Flights resumed at several major East Coast airports following a telecommunications disruption that resulted in disruptions for thousands of flights Monday. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted arrivals at major airports in New York, Boston and Philadelphia after the agency’s primary communication line in the region failed and railroad construction workers accidentally cut the backup…
articles.body:
Flights resumed at several major East Coast airports following a telecommunications disruption that resulted in disruptions for thousands of flights Monday.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted arrivals at major airports in New York, Boston and Philadelphia after the agency’s primary communication line in the region failed and railroad construction workers accidentally cut the backup fiber optic line.

In an update shared on social media late Monday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the telecom lines had been repaired and that “all airport operations” in the region would resume.

“It will take some time to clear all existing delays, so please check with your airline for the latest information,” he added.

Earlier on Monday, a replacement circuit had failed at the FAA’s Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control, leading transportation officials to find that the backup line was also inoperable.

Duffy initially stated that Amtrak workers were responsible for cutting the line, but Amtrak and NJ Transit disputed this claim.

NJ Transit said one of their construction crews inadvertently severed a fiber optic line while digging at a rail car storage site in the Garden State on Monday morning. In an update around 5:30 p.m. Monday, the agency said most of the fiber cables had been repaired and would be back online shortly.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford noted the “timing is absolutely horrible” and apologized for the delays and cancellations in comments to reporters on Monday.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to modernize the U.S. air traffic control system, including the type of primary circuit that failed in this outage.

Duffy has called on lawmakers to provide additional funding for the update projects.

“We still have problems, you’re right, but they’re not new to us,” the Transportation secretary told reporters on Monday, according to a video shared by CBS News. “We know what has to be fixed and it’s going to take partnership with the Congress to make it happen.”

The flight delays and cancellations occurred as world leaders arrived in New York City for the United Nations General Assembly this week. President Trump will address the international body on Tuesday morning.

articles.title: Almost 2 in 3 say US not winning Iran war: Survey
articles.summary: Almost 2 in 3 Americans said in a new poll that the United States is not winning the war in Iran and that President Trump is not doing enough to end the ongoing conflict. In the CNN and SSRS poll, released Tuesday, 64 percent of respondents said the U.S. is not winning the war in…
articles.body:
Almost 2 in 3 Americans said in a new poll that the United States is not winning the war in Iran and that President Trump is not doing enough to end the ongoing conflict.

In the CNN and SSRS poll , released Tuesday, 64 percent of respondents said the U.S. is not winning the war in Iran, while 36 percent disagreed.

The Iran conflict, which Trump initially said would end in roughly a month, has passed the six-month mark with no public signs of a deal to end hostilities. Trump earlier this month told reporters he believes the U.S. war with Iran will end “ immediately ” after November’s midterm elections.

He has also stated that he was weighing whether to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic’s regime or not.

“It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios on Thursday.

Seventy-eight percent of participants said the president is not doing enough to end the conflict with Iran, 22 percent responded he was and 1 percent had no opinion. Three-quarters also stated that Trump does not have a clear plan for handling the war.

The House passed a war powers resolution last week, limiting President Trump’s military actions in Iran. The resolution arrives as the cost of the war balloons to an estimated $2 billion per month, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office .

It marks the third time the House has passed a similar war powers resolution limiting Trump’s actions in the Iran war. But this time, the number of Republicans in support increased from four to seven.

According to the poll, negative attitudes among Democrats and independents have remained relatively unchanged throughout the conflict.

Republicans’ views, however, have dipped since March. Sixty percent of Republicans approved the way Trump was handling the war, marking a 13-point drop in six months.

The decline is also reflected in about half of Republicans who added that the president’s decision has helped the U.S.’s standing in the world, which is down 13 points since March.

The conflict has come with economic consequences for Americans, particularly at the pump, as gas prices have spiked as a result of restricted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The national average price of regular gas is roughly $4.47 per gallon as of Tuesday, according to AAA . That is about 36 cents higher than a month ago and roughly $1.50 greater than two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the war.

The CNN and SSRS took place from Sept. 16 to 17 and featured 1,206 respondents. Its margin of error was 3.5 percentage points.

articles.title: ‘Trump TV’ is just reruns of the president on YouTube
articles.summary: The White House has launched a new “Trump TV” livestream with 24/7 reruns of President Donald Trump’s speeches, bill signings, and other moments.
articles.body: The White House is now airing reruns of President Donald Trump’s speeches, bill signings, and other moments on a YouTube livestream that it’s calling “Trump TV,” as reported earlier by Time. The 24/7 station launched just days after Trump banned CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House. Following several teasers propping up “Trump TV,” Kaelan Dorr, the White House’s head of digital strategy, revealed that the administration will air Trump’s “greatest hits, unfiltered” on YouTube. “The press, in some cases, reported inaccurately or not at all on the Administration’s many record breaking accomplishments on behalf of all Americans,” Dorr writes. The White House also posted a promotion for the station featuring clips from various shows, like The Office, Seinfeld, and Family Guy. The livestream’s launch drew immediate criticism, with California Gov. Gavin Newsom calling it “state-run TV.” CNN, MS Now, and Politico also sued the Trump administration, claiming that their ban from the White House “threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” As reported by Time, CNN was supposed to shoot video for the press pool on Monday, but no other network took its place in support of the outlet. ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC later released a joint statement condemning the White House’s decision to ban a news organization because the administration “objects to its reporting.”

articles.title: What are Flock cameras, other ALPRs looking for?
articles.summary: You may have noticed more ALPRs around you. Here’s what they’re looking for.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Flock cameras, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and other similar devices have attracted backlash from around the country in recent months.

While Flock may be the name that immediately comes to mind for you when you hear of ALPRs, they aren’t the only technology available, nor the first of their kind.

They all, however, are generally looking for the same information. That includes a vehicle’s license plate and its make, model, and color.

Flock claims its readers can “capture vehicles traveling up to 100 MPH, day and night, and up to 75 ft away.” Its technology can also categorize vehicles based on whether it is a resident or non-resident vehicle, if it has a temporary or standard plate, and if there is damage or alterations, like a broken taillight.

While a Flock camera cannot determine if you are speeding, Genetec’s ALPR system is capable of providing the estimated travel speed of a vehicle.

Motorola Solutions , which comprises about 5 percent of the ALPR locations tracked by DeFlock, says its technology can identify “accessories and even unique vehicle features like damage or bumper stickers.”

Flock cameras “ take a point-in-time image of the rear of vehicles on public roadways,” so they aren’t able to track every vehicle or person in a jurisdiction, just capture the ones that pass in front of their view.

If you’re curious about which cameras are near you, you can take a look at DeFlock’s crowd-sourced map of ALPR locations around the U.S. “Camera locations come from volunteers and the OpenStreetMap community, not a private company or government agency,” DeFlock says.

You can zoom into the map above to explore the reported locations of cameras in your neighborhood, according to DeFlock’s crowdsourced data.

To open the map above in a new tab, click here .

Nexstar could not independently verify the camera locations.

ALPRs have been in use for “well over two decades,” according to a report from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. You can see ALPRs attached to poles, streetlights, and overpasses, though there are also mobile options available.

They’re capable of scanning license plates and comparing them in databases, which can then alert law enforcement if a sought-after vehicle is detected. Law enforcement can also review captures to search for vehicles and share information with other agencies.

However, some agencies have been instructed to stop using ALPRs. Communities in North Carolina , Indiana , Colorado , Wisconsin , and more have taken action to discontinue the use of such devices. The Florida Department of Transportation has started removing cameras from state highways and Texas has pulled state funding for the program following privacy concerns, misuse accusations, and, in Florida’s case, “ surveillance schemes .”

Despite the pushback some ALPRs have attracted, President Trump recently spoke out in favor of them .

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” Trump told reporters on Air Force One earlier this month when asked about Flock cameras, adding later, “I like them.”

articles.title: Fed’s Collins Says Rate Hike Will Help Return Inflation to Goal
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said she supported last week’s decision to raise interest rates, which she said would help bring infla...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said she supported last week's decision to raise interest rates, which she said would help bring inflation back to the central bank's 2% target.

"A somewhat more restrictive federal funds rate will help ensure that inflation durably returns to target," Collins wrote in a LinkedIn post on Tuesday. "With the labor market on a better footing, monetary policy can focus on a timely return to price stability, especially after five and a half years of too high inflation."

Collins, who doesn't vote on monetary policy this year, said she saw an "increased likelihood" of scenarios in which inflation remains "notably above 2%."

Fed officials voted unanimously last week to raise their benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point. In their updated economic projections, policymakers penciled in one more quarter-point hike this year, according to the median forecast. Eight officials forecast yet another increase in 2027.

Chairman Kevin Warsh, who again abstained from submitting rate projections, said last week's decision removes a "dose of accommodation" from the economy.

articles.title: Trump return to combat operations in Iran ‘inevitable’: Keane
articles.summary: Retired U.S. Army Gen. Jack Keane on Monday said it was “inevitable” that President Trump could resume combat operations against Iran as the conflict inches closer to the seven-month mark. Fox Business host Larry Kudlow asked Keane if Trump could resume fresh strikes on Tehran and whether the president should “deliver a stern warning” to…
articles.body:
Retired U.S. Army Gen. Jack Keane on Monday said it was “inevitable” that President Trump could resume combat operations against Iran as the conflict inches closer to the seven-month mark.

Fox Business host Larry Kudlow asked Keane if Trump could resume fresh strikes on Tehran and whether the president should “deliver a stern warning” to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York.

“Oh, I think combat operations are inevitable,” Keane answered. “And the reason is the mindset of the regime itself. They are determined here. They believe they can outlast us.”

“They believe their will is there, and that we have weakened as a result of what has taken place with oil spiking and the elections coming,” he continued.

The ex-general added that these were “real things” to not just the American people but also to Israeli voters heading to the polls in October. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who coordinated with U.S. officials in launching initial strikes on Iran in February, is running for reelection.

Keane added that the Iranian regime’s determination to stay in power and support its proxies , including the Houthis in Yemen, Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, will only fade “if we take away the centerpiece,” referring to Iran.

“I think combat operations, Larry, are inevitable,” he reiterated. “It’s a combination of the [U.S. Navy] blockade, the economic pressure [Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent’s putting on and –– yes –– significant combat operations conducted by Israel and the United States to finish this, to set the regime in a place with the right conditions for its collapse.”

Trump told world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday that he has a “big decision” coming on the U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran. He pondered if “the greatest in the Middle East or even the world” will be made with Iran or “do I annihilate the Islamic Republic.”

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said, later suggesting that a deal could be reached after the November midterm elections.

The Trump administration authorized visas for Iran’s delegation to the UNGA last week. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump was “open” to meeting with Pezeshkian and the rest of the delegation.

Military strikes between the U.S. and Iran resumed earlier this month after about six weeks of quiet. Iran targeted oil ships in the Strait of Hormuz , American bases in the region and U.S. allies. The Pentagon has fought back against the Islamic Republic’s control of the strait with a blockade on Iranian oil exports and struck military targets.

The effective shutdown of the waterway hit people globally with rising gas prices, a growing concern among voters worried about the cost of living and affordability ahead of November’s midterms. The national average for gas in the U.S. sat at $4.48 on Tuesday, while diesel was at $6.53, according to AAA .

articles.title: Stolen passwords are exposing America's water providers to hackers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Researchers say another looming threat hangs over some of America's most important critical infrastructure.
articles.body:
New security research has found that well over a thousand U.S. water and wastewater providers are exposed to hacks due to malware that’s capable of stealing their employees’ passwords and active logged-in sessions.

The findings by cybersecurity defense firm SpyCloud underscore how water providers and other critical infrastructure can be compromised with relative ease amidst a wave of hacks targeting the water supplies of dozens of communities across the United States.

While password-stealing malware is not new, the research highlights how stolen passwords offer hackers an easy route to break into an organization’s network without using AI tools.

SpyCloud said it built a database of more than 66,000 public-facing systems that are registered with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, amounting to 10,000 organizations. The company found password-stealing malware had swiped passwords and credentials from 1,787 organizations, or nearly two in 10 providers they checked. The firm noted at least 250 organizations had credentials exposed that appeared to allow access to their operational networks and remote-access systems, which control the physical pumps and water flows.

The analysis covered an unnamed metering tech provider, which had a device on its network that was infected with password-stealing malware. The malware stole reams of credentials, including passwords for 167 U.S. utility companies that rely on the metering tech provider.

SpyCloud Chief Investigations Officer Jason Lancaster said in the post that this single breach handed criminals the keys to access “a hundred otherwise unrelated organizations.”

Password-stealing malware, also known as infostealers , allows hackers to steal a person’s stored passwords as well as the session tokens that are used to keep them logged in. These session tokens can allow a hacker to log in as if they were the legitimate user, and can often bypass multi-factor authentication systems. Hackers regularly trade stolen credentials in order to obtain passwords or session tokens for accessing specific organizations.

This research comes weeks after a spate of hacks targeting water providers around the United States, which the U.S. government has privately tied to Iran-backed hackers . SpyCloud said it found no evidence that those Iran-linked hacks relied on stolen passwords. In those cases, the signs point to security weaknesses, such as manufacturer-set default passwords, in the mechanical switches and physical controllers used by critical infrastructure, SpyCloud said, echoing earlier findings from U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA.

Rather, the researchers note that stolen passwords are a major source of access to “whoever wants to buy or find it,” in parallel to the known security risks with critical infrastructure tech. Lancaster said that the water-sector “has to hold both stories at once.”

articles.title: Waymo drives through Denver farmers market during setup
articles.summary: New video shows a Waymo robotaxi driving down a closed road and through a Denver farmers market.
articles.body:
DENVER ( KDVR ) — New video shows a Waymo robotaxi driving down a closed road and through a Denver farmers market.

At about 8:15 a.m. Sunday, 160 vendors were setting up at the South Pearl Street Farmers Market when the self-driving vehicle came through.

“It entered through our food truck area,” said Nicole Jarman, the production director of the farmers market.

Jarman said there was a “Road Closed” sign on one side of the street, but the other side of the street was still open to vendor traffic during setup, and the Waymo followed a vendor vehicle past the sign and then turned onto the 1400 block of South Pearl Street.

“It’s still load-in, our barricades are moved to the side, so there’s vehicular access, and it followed that traffic, went slow, and then made its way on out at Arkansas and kept going,” she said.

“It was not anything that made us nervous,” Jarman said.

No one was hurt, but the incident does bring up safety concerns surrounding Waymo.

The company said the autonomous vehicle was navigating to an address on Pearl Street, quickly identified the situation and maneuvered out of the market area.

A spokesperson offered a statement, saying, “The trust and safety of the community is our top priority. We are dedicated to learning from this situation as we continue improving road safety in the cities we serve.”

Waymo began letting the public book rides in Denver earlier this month.

The company said its vehicles are designed to adapt to dynamic conditions, and the vehicles drive millions of autonomous miles a week, achieving 94% fewer serious injury accidents than human drivers.
